I thought so. Okay. So wouldn't that mean C is a better choice than C++ to start? I'm curious myself cuz i've been meaning to branch off beyong python and ruby.

That depends. C is in many ways a simpler language than C++, in the raw sense of being “smaller”, having less features, and it is thus easier to learn.

However, C is also lower level, and a lot of abstractions which are offered by C++ are simply not present or not even possible (cheaply, especially in terms of syntax). This makes it harder to use, especially when more complex data structures are involved.

C++ on the other hand is huge, has a lot of core features that C doesn't have, and a very rich standard library that makes it more comfortable to approach for people coming from higher language.

Some good advise in here already, so I won't repeat that. Just wanted to add two things:

1) With code changes, start small and work up. If you're ultimate goal is to get your code into the system, start with small things that you can safely contribute, then plan on working your way up. Don't try to redesign/reimplement some massive or critical portion of a popular project.

2) In the short-term, remember there are a lot of non-coding tasks that need to get done. As one person mentioned, doing deep-dives into bug reports is one way to help. Actively testing (not just using and reporting) is another. But if you've got any language skills, documentation is one of those areas that always needs another set of hands. Heck, even just hanging out in their troubleshooting forums and helping out new users will be of immense value (and will undoubtedly help you become more familiar with the details of the project).
